name: Infinite scroll
definition: A list that appends the next page of results automatically as the reader approaches the bottom, so the content never ends and no page controls appear.
useWhen: the feed loads more by itself as you near the bottom

sources.title: NN/g: Infinite Scrolling: When to Use It, When to Avoid It

notes: The accessibility complaint (unreachable footer) is the false-bottom term, kept separate.

name: Pagination
definition: Splitting a long result set into numbered pages the reader steps through, so each page has a stable address and a known position in the whole.
useWhen: results are cut into numbered pages you can jump between

sources.title: NN/g: Alternatives to Pagination on Product-Listing Pages

notes: Most design systems file pagination as a component; recorded here as the flow pattern, merge step should pick one home.

name: Load more
definition: A button at the end of a list that fetches and appends the next batch only when pressed, keeping the reader in control of how much arrives.
useWhen: the next batch waits behind a button instead of arriving on its own

sources.title: NN/g: Alternatives to Pagination on Product-Listing Pages

name: Cursor pagination
definition: Paging that moves by a pointer into the result set rather than a page number, so newly inserted rows never shift what the next page contains.
useWhen: the list only offers next and previous, never page numbers
notes: Names the reason a feed shows only Next and Previous. Sits on the boundary between data access and UI vocabulary.

name: Pull to refresh
definition: Dragging a list downward past its top edge to trigger a reload, with a spinner that appears in the space the drag opens up.
useWhen: tugging a list down to fetch new items
notes: Credited to Loren Brichter's Tweetie; worth a history note in the article.

name: Lazy loading
definition: Deferring the fetch of an image, list section, or module until it is about to be needed, usually when it approaches the viewport.
useWhen: content is fetched only once it is nearly on screen

name: List virtualization
definition: Rendering only the rows currently in view and a small buffer around them, while spacers preserve the scrollbar of the full list.
useWhen: a huge list renders only the rows you can see
notes: Breaks find-in-page and anchor links, which is the usual reason a reader goes looking for the word.

name: Progressive image loading
definition: Showing a cheap stand-in for an image, a blur, a dominant colour, or a low resolution copy, and swapping in the full file once it arrives.
useWhen: a blurred or coloured block stands in until the photo loads
notes: Contrast with skeleton-screen (already on site): skeletons stand in for layout, LQIP stands in for one image.

name: Undo
definition: Letting an action run immediately and offering to reverse it afterwards, instead of stopping to ask whether the reader really meant it.
useWhen: the action happens first and offers a way back

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Undos instead of prompting for confirmation

name: Soft delete
definition: Removing an item from view but keeping it recoverable in a trash or archive for a period, so deletion is reversible without a confirmation step.
useWhen: deleted things go to a bin you can dig them out of

name: Type to confirm
definition: Guarding a destructive action by making the reader type the name of the thing being destroyed before the confirm button becomes usable.
useWhen: you must type the repo name to delete it
notes: GitHub popularised it; Cloudscape documents it as delete with text confirmation.

name: Wizard
definition: A task broken into ordered steps with only one step visible at a time, plus a fixed indicator of how many steps remain.
useWhen: a long task is walked through one screen at a time
notes: Naming split worth recording: wizard is the flow, stepper is the indicator component.

name: Steps left
definition: Telling the reader where they are in a multi-step task and how many steps are still to come, so the end of the task is visible from the start.
useWhen: the flow says step 2 of 5

name: One thing per page
definition: Asking a single question on each screen of a form so the reader never chooses which field to answer first and errors point somewhere unambiguous.
useWhen: each form screen asks exactly one question
notes: GOV.UK files it as Question pages; the phrase one thing per page is the community headword.

name: Check answers
definition: A review screen listing everything the reader entered, with a change link beside each answer, shown before the submission is final.
useWhen: a summary screen lets you review and edit before submitting

name: Confirmation page
definition: The screen that closes a transaction, stating plainly that it succeeded, giving a reference the reader can quote, and saying what happens next.
useWhen: the screen that says it worked and what happens next

name: Error summary
definition: A block at the top of a failed form listing every problem as links that move focus to the field that caused it.
useWhen: one list at the top links to each broken field

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System: Recover from validation errors

notes: Could land in accessibility instead; the focus-management behaviour is the whole point of it.

name: Inline validation
definition: Checking a field as the reader leaves or fills it and showing the verdict next to that field, rather than saving all complaints for submission.
useWhen: a field tells you it is wrong before you submit

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Inline Validation instead of delaying errors

name: Inline edit
definition: Turning a piece of displayed content into an editable field in place, so the reader changes it without leaving the page or opening a form.
useWhen: clicking the text itself turns it into a field

name: Autosave
definition: Persisting the reader's work continuously without a save action, usually with a quiet status line reporting when the last save happened.
useWhen: work is kept without anyone pressing save

name: Unsaved changes guard
definition: Warning the reader that edits will be lost before a navigation or close is allowed to proceed, and offering to save or discard first.
useWhen: leaving a form asks whether to discard your edits

name: Drag to reorder
definition: Changing the order of a list by dragging an item to a new position, with the remaining items shifting to show where it will land.
useWhen: you rearrange a list by dragging its rows
notes: The keyboard equivalent (move up, move down, or grab and arrow) is the accessibility half of this term.

name: Drop indicator
definition: The line or highlighted gap drawn during a drag to show exactly where the item will land if it is released now.
useWhen: the line that shows where the dragged item will land
notes: Strong long-tail candidate: people search for the name of the blue line.

name: Drag preview
definition: The semi-transparent copy of the dragged item that follows the pointer, sometimes collapsed into a stack when several items move at once.
useWhen: the ghost of the item that follows your cursor

name: Bulk actions
definition: Selecting several rows and applying one command to all of them, usually through a bar that appears once a selection exists and reports its count.
useWhen: picking many rows and acting on them at once

name: Select all across pages
definition: Offering to extend a selection from the visible page to every matching row, after a header checkbox has selected only what is on screen.
useWhen: select all offers to also take the rows you cannot see
notes: Gmail popularised the two-stage version; no design system seems to have a documented name for it.

name: Range selection
definition: Clicking one item then shift-clicking another to select everything between them, the keyboard-modified alternative to ticking each row.
useWhen: shift-click grabs everything between two rows
notes: Could belong in interaction; recorded here because it is a selection model rather than a gesture.
resolved: folded into range-select, which carries "range selection"

name: Marquee selection
definition: Dragging a rectangle across empty space to select every item it touches, the desktop file manager gesture carried into canvases and boards.
useWhen: dragging a box across items to select them
notes: Prime long-tail entry: several competing names and no authoritative documentation.
resolved: folded into lasso-selection, which carries "marquee selection"

name: Faceted search
definition: Narrowing results by ticking values from several independent attribute groups, with counts showing how many results each value would leave.
useWhen: filters grouped by attribute, each showing result counts

sources.title: A List Apart: Design Patterns: Faceted Navigation

name: Applied filters
definition: A row of removable tokens above the results showing every filter currently in force, with a control to clear them all at once.
useWhen: the removable tags showing which filters are on
notes: chip already exists on the site; this is the pattern that uses chips, so it needs a contrastWith edge rather than a merge.

name: Typeahead
definition: Offering suggestions that update on every keystroke, drawn from a live query, so the reader picks a result rather than finishing the phrase.
useWhen: suggestions appear and change as you type
notes: combobox is already on the site as the component; typeahead is the behaviour, and the two need a disambiguation article.

name: Inline autocomplete
definition: Completing the reader's text inside the field itself, with the guessed remainder selected so the next keystroke replaces it.
useWhen: the field finishes your word inside the field

implementations.name: Editable Combobox With Both List and Inline Autocomplete

notes: Ghost text now also names the AI completion suggestion in editors; a naming collision worth an article.

name: Did you mean
definition: Offering a corrected spelling for a query that returned little or nothing, either as a suggestion to accept or as a substitution the reader can undo.
useWhen: search offers a corrected spelling of your query
notes: The forgiving reading of it (auto-substitute plus a way back) is the interesting half.

name: No results state
definition: What a search or filtered list shows when nothing matched, naming the query, explaining why, and offering a way to loosen the constraints.
useWhen: the screen shown when a search matches nothing
notes: empty-state and zero-state already exist on the site. This is the distinct no-results reading; if the merge step folds it in, keep no results and zero results as aliases there.

name: Onboarding tour
definition: A short sequence of pointers layered over a live interface, each naming one control, advanced by the reader and skippable at any point.
useWhen: a stepped overlay walks you around a live screen

name: Coach mark
definition: A translucent overlay drawn once over a first run, labelling controls with hand-drawn arrows and captions and dismissed by a single tap anywhere.
useWhen: the one-time scribbled overlay labelling the whole screen
notes: Distinct from a tour: one screen, all at once, no steps. Widely conflated, which is exactly why the entry earns its place.

name: Hotspot
definition: A small pulsing dot placed on a control to advertise that something can be learned there, expanding into a tip when the reader engages with it.
useWhen: the pulsing dot inviting you to discover a feature
resolved: folded into coach-mark, which carries "hotspot" and "beacon"

name: Onboarding checklist
definition: A persistent list of setup tasks with completion state and a progress meter, kept available so the reader can return to unfinished steps.
useWhen: a setup list you can leave and come back to

sources.title: GOV.UK Design System: Complete multiple tasks

notes: GOV.UK renamed Task list pages to Complete multiple tasks and split out a Task list component; both names are live in the wild.

name: Endowed progress
definition: Starting a progress meter part filled, so the reader feels they are continuing something already begun rather than starting from nothing.
useWhen: the progress bar starts at 20 percent before you did anything

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Upfront Progress instead of starting with a blank

name: Goal gradient
definition: Effort rising as a visible goal gets closer, which is why interfaces show how little is left rather than how much has been done.
useWhen: the interface shows how close you are, not how far you came
notes: A psychology principle rather than a UI shape; kept because its interface expression (a nearly full meter) is demoable.

name: Swipe to reveal
definition: Sliding a list row sideways to uncover a strip of actions behind it, which stay open until one is chosen or the row is slid back.
useWhen: sliding a row aside uncovers its hidden buttons

sources.title: NN/g: Using Swipe to Trigger Contextual Actions

notes: Reveal mode versus execute mode is the useful distinction: execute fires the action once the swipe passes a threshold.
resolved: folded into swipe-actions, which carries "swipe to reveal"

name: Swipe to dismiss
definition: Flinging an item off the edge of the screen to remove it, with the item tracking the finger and snapping back if the throw is too short.
useWhen: throwing a card or notification off the screen to clear it

sources.title: NN/g: Using Swipe to Trigger Contextual Actions

name: Swipe deck
definition: A stack of cards judged one at a time, each thrown left or right to record a binary decision and reveal the next card underneath.
useWhen: a stack of cards you swipe left or right to judge
notes: No design system documents it; the vernacular name is the product that popularised it.

name: List detail
definition: A list of items beside the full record of whichever one is selected, collapsing to a single navigable pane when the screen is too narrow for both.
useWhen: a list on one side and the selected item's detail on the other
notes: Arguably layout rather than pattern; the responsive collapse behaviour is what makes it a flow. Android renamed master-detail to list-detail, a naming shift worth an article.

name: Priority plus navigation
definition: A horizontal menu that keeps as many items visible as fit and moves the rest into a More control, recalculating whenever the available width changes.
useWhen: the nav shows what fits and hides the rest behind More
notes: Coined by Michael Scharnagl, popularised by Brad Frost. overflow-menu already exists on the site as the component; this is the responsive strategy that fills it.

name: Quick return header
definition: A header that slides out of the way while the reader scrolls down and returns immediately on the first upward scroll, without waiting for the top of the page.
useWhen: the bar hides going down and comes back the moment you scroll up

sources.title: Bram.us: hide a header when scrolling down, show it again when scrolling up

notes: iframe demo: the subject is the document scroller and a position:sticky header measured against it.

name: Back to top
definition: A control that appears after the reader has scrolled some distance and returns them to the top of the page in one action.
useWhen: the button that appears partway down to send you back up
notes: iframe demo: the trigger threshold is a property of the document scroller.

name: Reading progress
definition: A bar tied to scroll position that shows how much of an article remains, usually pinned to the top edge and filling as the reader descends.
useWhen: the thin bar showing how far through the article you are
notes: iframe demo: the subject is scroll-driven animation over the document scroller. scroll-spy already exists and should carry a contrastWith edge.

name: Scroll hijacking
definition: Overriding the browser's scrolling so a wheel turn advances a scripted sequence instead of moving the page by the distance the reader asked for.
useWhen: the page takes over what one scroll of the wheel does
notes: Almost always used pejoratively; contrast with scroll-snap, which constrains scrolling without stealing it.

name: False bottom
definition: A page that looks finished at a point where content actually continues, so the reader stops scrolling and never sees the rest.
useWhen: the page looks like it ended but has not

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Suggesting Continuity instead of false bottoms

notes: Excellent long-tail entry: readers know the problem and not the word.

name: Permission priming
definition: Explaining why access is needed in the product's own dialog first, and only firing the operating system prompt once the reader has said yes to that.
useWhen: your own dialog asks before the real system prompt does
notes: Genuine long-tail gold: three competing names for one well-understood behaviour.

name: Interstitial
definition: A full screen placed between two steps of a flow, carrying a message, an advert, or a warning that the reader must pass through to continue.
useWhen: a whole screen sits between you and where you were going

name: Smart app banner
definition: A strip pinned to the top of a mobile web page urging the reader to open or install the native app instead, with an install or open action.
useWhen: the strip on a mobile site pushing you into the app
notes: The full-screen version is penalised by search engines as an intrusive interstitial, which is part of the term's story.

name: Rating prompt
definition: An in-product request to rate or review, usually timed to a moment of success and often filtered so only positive responses reach the public store.
useWhen: the app asks how you like it right after something went well
notes: Review gating (routing unhappy answers to private feedback) is against both app store policies, worth saying in the article.

name: Microsurvey
definition: A one or two question survey placed inside the product at the moment being asked about, answered in place rather than on a separate page.
useWhen: a one-question survey inside the thing it asks about

name: Paywall
definition: A barrier that stops access to content or a feature until the reader pays, placed either before anything is shown or partway into the content.
useWhen: the point where content stops until you pay

name: Metered paywall
definition: A paywall that grants a fixed number of free items per period and counts down publicly, so the barrier arrives only after the reader is invested.
useWhen: you get three free articles a month and a counter says so
notes: The fade-to-white teaser above it is a separate visual device, sometimes called a content fade or gradient fade.

name: Feature gate
definition: Showing a locked feature in place, with its real position in the interface, so the reader sees what upgrading would unlock rather than a hidden absence.
useWhen: a locked feature stays visible with an upgrade badge

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Exposing Options instead of hiding them

name: Lazy registration
definition: Letting someone use a product and accumulate state anonymously, and asking for an account only when that state needs to survive the session.
useWhen: you can start using it before making an account

name: Gradual engagement
definition: Replacing a sign-up form at the front door with a first useful action, so the reader experiences value before being asked for anything.
useWhen: the first screen does something instead of asking you to register

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Gradual Engagement instead of a hasty sign up

name: Progressive profiling
definition: Collecting profile details a few at a time across separate visits, instead of demanding the whole record in one long form at registration.
useWhen: the product asks for one more detail each time you return

name: Social login
definition: Signing in by delegating identity to an existing account elsewhere, presented as a row of provider buttons above or instead of a password form.
useWhen: the row of continue with Google and Apple buttons
notes: The NASCAR problem (too many provider buttons) is the usual reason people search for this term.

name: Magic link
definition: Signing in by clicking a single-use link emailed on request, with no password, and a screen that waits and offers to resend while the mail arrives.
useWhen: you sign in by clicking a link sent to your email
notes: The waiting screen with a resend timer is the demoable half of the term.

name: One-time code login
definition: Signing in by typing a short code sent to a second channel, keeping the reader inside the app rather than sending them out to a mail client.
useWhen: you type a six digit code sent by mail or text
notes: The segmented code input is a component (pin input, one-time code field); this record is the flow around it.

name: Passkey
definition: Signing in with a device-held credential unlocked by the reader's own biometric or screen lock, so the interface asks for a face or fingerprint, not a secret.
useWhen: signing in with a fingerprint instead of a password
notes: demo none: the interesting part is an operating system dialog that cannot be reproduced honestly in a page.

name: Password strength meter
definition: A gauge that scores a password while it is typed and names what would improve it, replacing a list of rules with continuous feedback.
useWhen: the bar that rates a password as you type it

name: Reveal password
definition: A toggle inside a password field that switches the text between masked and readable, so the reader can check what they typed before submitting.
useWhen: the eye icon that unmasks what you typed
notes: The crossed-eye icon means the opposite thing in different products, a genuine and documented ambiguity.
resolved: folded into password-reveal-toggle, which carries "reveal password" and "show password toggle"

name: Captcha
definition: A challenge inserted into a flow to distinguish a person from a script, ranging from distorted text to a single checkbox judged by behaviour.
useWhen: the step that proves you are not a robot

name: Honeypot field
definition: A form field hidden from people but visible to automated form fillers, used to reject submissions that fill it in without challenging anyone.
useWhen: the invisible field that only a bot would fill in
notes: Cross-cuts accessibility: a naive display:none honeypot is invisible to screen readers too, which is why the correct technique matters.

name: Cookie consent banner
definition: A notice asking permission to store non-essential cookies before the reader has done anything, offering accept, reject, and a route to per-purpose choices.
useWhen: the consent notice that greets you before you read anything
notes: banner already exists on the site as the component. This is the flow, and it is where several deceptive design terms live in the wild.

name: Guest checkout
definition: Letting a buyer complete a purchase without creating an account, with the offer to save details moved to after the order is placed.
useWhen: buying without being made to create an account

name: Express checkout
definition: A row of one-tap payment buttons placed above the normal form, which fetch address and payment details from a wallet the buyer already has.
useWhen: the wallet buttons above the checkout form

name: Order summary
definition: The persistent panel beside a checkout listing items, quantities, and every cost line, kept visible so nothing about the total arrives as a surprise.
useWhen: the panel beside checkout that itemises what you will pay

name: Address autocomplete
definition: Replacing a set of address fields with one lookup that suggests full addresses after a few characters and fills the rest on selection.
useWhen: typing a postcode fills in the whole address

name: Sticky add to cart
definition: A condensed product bar that pins itself to an edge once the real buy button has scrolled away, keeping price and purchase always reachable.
useWhen: the buy bar that sticks once the real button scrolls off
notes: iframe demo: it is defined by its relationship to the document scroller.

name: Mini cart
definition: A compact view of the basket opened from the cart icon, confirming what was just added and offering checkout without leaving the current page.
useWhen: the small basket panel that opens from the cart icon
notes: drawer already exists as the component; this is the commerce reading of it.

name: Save for later
definition: Moving an item out of the active list into a parked list that stays associated with the reader, without deleting it or committing to it.
useWhen: parking an item without buying or discarding it

name: Quick view
definition: Opening a summary of an item over the list it came from, so the reader can inspect it and return without losing scroll position or filters.
useWhen: peeking at an item without leaving the list
notes: hover-card already exists; quick view is the deliberate open, not the hover.

name: Social proof
definition: Showing what other people did or said next to a decision, as counts, reviews, logos, or live activity, so the reader can borrow their judgement.
useWhen: the interface shows what others chose to steady your choice

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Social Proof instead of talking about yourself

name: Scarcity indicator
definition: A label reporting how little of something is left, in stock, in seats, or in time, placed beside the action it is meant to accelerate.
useWhen: only two left in stock, printed next to the buy button
notes: Honest when the number is real; the fabricated version is recorded separately as fake-scarcity.

name: Countdown timer
definition: A running clock attached to an offer or a held resource, showing how long remains and what will happen when it reaches zero.
useWhen: a clock ticking down beside an offer or a held seat

name: Session timeout warning
definition: A dialog that appears before an idle session expires, counting down and offering to extend it, so unsaved work is not lost silently.
useWhen: the warning that you are about to be signed out
notes: Accessibility overlap: WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable is what forces the extend option.
resolved: folded into timeout-warning, which carries "session timeout warning"

name: Streak
definition: A count of consecutive periods in which the reader did the thing, displayed prominently and lost if a period is missed.
useWhen: the running count of consecutive days you kept going
notes: Loss aversion made visible; the streak freeze is the mitigation and is itself a named sub-pattern.

name: Leaderboard
definition: A ranked list of participants by some score, with the reader's own position pinned into view even when it falls outside the visible range.
useWhen: a ranked table with your own row pinned into view

name: Achievement badge
definition: A collectible marker awarded for a milestone and displayed on a profile, often shown greyed out before it is earned so the set is visible.
useWhen: the collectible award shown on a profile
notes: badge already exists on the site as the small count or status marker; this is the gamification sense and needs a contrastWith edge, not a merge.

name: Dark pattern
definition: An interface arranged to make the reader do something they did not intend and would not have chosen, by exploiting how attention and defaults work.
useWhen: the interface is designed against the person using it

sources.title: Deceptive Design: Types of deceptive pattern

notes: Harry Brignull coined dark pattern in 2010 and now prefers deceptive pattern; the rename is the article. Parent term for the whole family below.

name: Confirmshaming
definition: Wording the decline option so that choosing it is an admission of something embarrassing, making refusal feel like a confession rather than a choice.
useWhen: the no button is written to make you feel bad

aliases.name: no thanks, I hate saving money

name: Roach motel
definition: Making entry into a commitment take one click and exit take a phone call, a chat queue, or a buried page, so the asymmetry keeps people subscribed.
useWhen: easy to sign up, deliberately hard to leave
notes: deceptive.design renamed it Hard to cancel; roach motel remains the searched term, which is exactly the kind of gap this site should close.

name: Drip pricing
definition: Advertising a low headline price and adding mandatory fees one screen at a time, so the true total only appears once the buyer is committed.
useWhen: fees keep appearing as you move through checkout

name: Sneak into basket
definition: Adding an item the buyer never chose, an insurance, a donation, a warranty, into the cart through a preselected control found earlier in the flow.
useWhen: something you never picked is in your basket

name: Privacy zuckering
definition: Steering people into sharing more about themselves than they meant to, by making the permissive choice the easy one and the private choice several clicks deep.
useWhen: the settings are arranged so sharing is the easy answer

sources.title: Deceptive Design: Types of deceptive pattern

notes: Named after Mark Zuckerberg; still in Brignull's original twelve but absorbed into other categories on the current types index. Verify before publishing.

name: Nagging
definition: Interrupting a task again and again with the same request, so that agreeing becomes the cheapest way to be left alone.
useWhen: the same prompt keeps returning until you give in

name: Disguised ad
definition: An advertisement styled to look like a control or an item of content, so the click it collects was aimed at something else entirely.
useWhen: the download button that is actually an advert

name: Preselected opt-in
definition: Arriving at a choice with the answer that benefits the business already ticked, so consent is collected from everyone who does not notice.
useWhen: the marketing box is already ticked when you get there
notes: Sharpest contrast pair on the site: smart-defaults and preselected-opt-in are the same mechanic judged by whose interest the default serves.

name: Forced continuity
definition: Turning a free trial into a paid subscription automatically, with the card taken up front and no reminder before the first real charge.
useWhen: a free trial quietly becomes a paid plan

name: Misdirection
definition: Using contrast, size, and position to pull attention to the option the business prefers while the other option is present but visually demoted.
useWhen: the choice you want is there but styled to be missed

name: Fake scarcity
definition: Claiming limited supply that is not real, with stock counts or demand messages generated to pressure a decision rather than report a fact.
useWhen: only three left, and the number is invented

name: Fake urgency
definition: Presenting a deadline that does not exist, usually a timer that resets on reload, so the reader hurries a decision they had time to make.
useWhen: the countdown resets when you refresh the page

name: Fake social proof
definition: Manufacturing evidence that other people approve, through invented reviews, testimonials, or live activity messages nobody actually generated.
useWhen: someone in Leeds just bought this, and nobody did

name: Trick wording
definition: Phrasing a choice so its plain reading is the opposite of its effect, typically through double negatives or a label that describes the wrong outcome.
useWhen: untick this box to not stop receiving emails

name: Comparison prevention
definition: Structuring plans or products so their features and prices cannot be lined up, forcing a decision that no side-by-side reading would support.
useWhen: the plans are built so you cannot compare them

name: Obstruction
definition: Putting deliberate hurdles in front of an action the business does not want taken, so the effort itself does the discouraging.
useWhen: the path exists but is made exhausting on purpose
notes: Not all added friction is deceptive: type-to-confirm is deliberate friction in the reader's favour, which makes a good contrast pair.

name: Friend spam
definition: Asking for access to a contact list under one pretext and using it to send invitations that appear to come from the reader.
useWhen: the app mails your contacts as if you had
notes: One of Brignull's original twelve. The honest version (invite friends) and the deceptive version share a shape, which is the article.

name: Activity feed
definition: A reverse chronological list of things that happened, each entry naming an actor, a verb, and an object, grouped when many are alike.
useWhen: the running list of who did what, most recent first

name: Stories
definition: A sequence of full-screen cards that advance on a timer, paused by holding, skipped by tapping the edges, and gone after a fixed lifetime.
useWhen: the timed full-screen cards you tap through
notes: The segmented progress bar along the top is a component-level term of its own and may deserve a separate entry.

name: Mention autocomplete
definition: Typing a trigger character inside a text field to open a filtered list of people or objects, inserting the chosen one as a linked token.
useWhen: typing @ opens a list of people to insert
notes: Distinguished from slash-command by what selection does: a mention inserts text, a slash command runs something.

name: Slash command
definition: Typing a forward slash in a composer to open a menu of actions, where choosing one runs it rather than inserting the words into the message.
useWhen: typing / in the message box opens a command menu

name: Typing indicator
definition: A transient signal that someone else is composing a message, usually three animated dots, which disappears if they stop or send.
useWhen: the three bouncing dots meaning someone is replying
notes: Now doubles as the waiting state for a language model reply, which is a live naming collision worth documenting.

name: Read receipt
definition: A per-message marker reporting how far a message got, sent, delivered, or read, drawn as ticks, labels, or the recipient's avatar.
useWhen: the ticks that say sent, delivered, and read
notes: The double tick and its colour are conventions with no standard, so the term is understood but the drawing is not.

name: Presence indicator
definition: A small marker attached to a person showing whether they are available right now, and the faces or cursors of everyone currently in a shared document.
useWhen: the dot or avatar row saying who is here right now
notes: Facepile and avatar group are component names; presence is the pattern that gives them meaning.

name: Notification digest
definition: Collecting many similar alerts into one summary rather than delivering each, so the count rises but the number of interruptions does not.
useWhen: many alerts arrive as one grouped summary
notes: Android says group and summary notification; Apple says notification summary. Both names are live.

name: Feature spotlight
definition: A one-time announcement pointing at something newly added, shown in place next to the feature and dismissed for good once acknowledged.
useWhen: the one-time New badge pointing at a change

name: First run experience
definition: Everything shown only on the very first open, from a welcome sequence to seeded sample content, and never shown to that person again.
useWhen: what happens only the very first time you open it
notes: FRE and FTUE are widely used inside product teams and almost never written down, which makes this a strong dictionary entry.

name: Keyboard shortcut overlay
definition: A panel of every available shortcut, opened by a shortcut of its own and grouped by context, that closes on the next key press.
useWhen: pressing ? shows the list of every shortcut
resolved: folded into keyboard-shortcuts-dialog, which carries "keyboard shortcut overlay"

name: Help drawer
definition: Documentation opened beside the task rather than over it, keeping the form usable while the explanation is read and staying open across steps.
useWhen: help opens beside the form instead of on top of it

name: Forgiving format
definition: Accepting whatever shape the reader types and normalising it afterwards, instead of rejecting input that differs only in spacing or punctuation.
useWhen: the field takes the card number however you type it

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Forgiving Inputs instead of being strict with data

name: Structured format
definition: Splitting one value across several small fields with fixed shapes, which teaches the expected format but costs the reader extra focus moves.
useWhen: one value split across several little boxes

name: Input mask
definition: Formatting a value inside the field as it is typed, inserting separators automatically so the shape of the value is visible while entering it.
useWhen: the field adds the dashes and spaces as you type
notes: Widely considered harmful for phone numbers and welcome for card numbers; the disagreement is the article.

name: Smart defaults
definition: Prefilling a choice with the answer most people in this situation want, so the common case needs no work and every other case is still reachable.
useWhen: the form arrives already answered the way you would have

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Smart Defaults instead of asking to do extra work

name: Offline indicator
definition: A persistent notice that the product has lost its connection, saying what still works, what is queued, and when the last sync happened.
useWhen: the bar telling you the app is working offline
notes: Pairs with optimistic-ui (already on site): optimistic UI is what fills the gap this indicator explains.

name: Direct manipulation
definition: Acting on an object by handling the object itself, dragging, resizing, or typing into it, rather than describing the change in a separate control.
useWhen: you change the thing by grabbing the thing

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Direct Manipulation instead of contextless menus

notes: Ben Shneiderman's term from 1982; the history is worth a paragraph.

name: Morphing control
definition: One control that changes what it says and does according to state, showing play when paused and pause when playing rather than offering both.
useWhen: one button that becomes the next action each time

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Multifunctional Controls instead of more parts

notes: Accessibility trap worth naming: a morphing label breaks the promise that a control's name describes what it does.

name: Progressive reduction
definition: Simplifying a control as the same person uses it more, dropping the label once the icon has been learned and restoring it after a long absence.
useWhen: the label falls away once you have used it enough

sources.title: GoodUI: Try Progressive Reduction instead of being static

notes: Coined at Dan Birman and Allan Grinshtein's LayerVault; more discussed than shipped, which is itself worth saying.

name: Hub and spoke
definition: A navigation shape where every task is reached from one home screen and returns to it, with no way to move sideways between tasks.
useWhen: every section is reached from home and returns there
notes: Cross-category: could be filed as layout. The original iOS home screen is the canonical example.

name: Zebra striping
definition: Tinting alternate rows of a table so the eye can track one record across many columns without losing the line.
useWhen: alternating row tints to keep your place across columns
notes: Cross-category candidate: could sit in color or layout. The evidence that it helps is weaker than its popularity suggests, which is worth saying.

name: Expandable row
definition: A table row that opens in place to show detail beneath it, keeping the surrounding rows and the reader's scroll position intact.
useWhen: a row opens downward to show its details
notes: accordion already exists on the site; this is the table reading of it and needs a contrastWith edge.

name: Sticky column
definition: Holding the identifying column in place while the rest of a wide table scrolls sideways, so every row stays labelled at any horizontal position.
useWhen: the first column stays put while the table scrolls sideways
resolved: folded into frozen-column, the table sense this record defines, while sticky-sidebar owns the "sticky column" spelling for the layout sense

name: Comparison table
definition: A grid with options as columns and attributes as rows, aligned so the same attribute reads across every option and differences are visible at a glance.
useWhen: options as columns, features as rows, lined up to compare

sources.title: UX Patterns for Developers: Comparison Table

name: Rule builder
definition: Assembling a condition from dropdowns and values, joined by and or or, so a non-programmer can express a query without writing one.
useWhen: building an if-this-then-that condition from dropdowns

name: Drill-down navigation
definition: Going deeper into a hierarchy one level at a time inside the same panel, each level replacing the last and offering a way back up.
useWhen: a hierarchy is too deep to show all at once
notes: The mobile settings pattern, and the one a narrow sidebar falls back to. The state question worth writing about is whether the panel you came from keeps its scroll and form state when you go back.

name: Microcopy
definition: An interface's smallest strings: the verb on the button, the line under the field, the sentence when it fails. Short enough to be read every time.
useWhen: the words a control needs to be understood, not the prose around it

sources.title: NN/g: The 3 I's of Microcopy, Inform, Influence, and Interact
NN/g: UX Copy Sizes, Long, Short, and Micro
NN/g: The 3 C's of Informational Microcopy
Kinneret Yifrah, Microcopy: The Complete Guide (2nd edition)

notes: THE LARGEST HOLE this sweep found: 1,114 published terms and not one word for the words. The site already defines a dozen instances of microcopy (error-message, helper-text, empty-state, no-results-state, placeholder-as-label, confirmshaming) and had no name for the class. FENCE: this is the CLASS, never the instances, so it must never claim 'helper text'/'hint text'/'supporting text' (helper-text), 'inline error'/'validation message' (error-message), or 'placeholder text' (lorem-ipsum). 'UX writing' is carried as an alias on Yifrah's own ruling that the two are synonyms; NN/g's definitional boundary is the useful one for the article, copy shorter than three sentences that is read more often than anything else on the screen. Specimen: one form twice, the platform's default strings against authored ones, which is the whole term in a single still. Both unverified implementation rows are JS-rendered shells that answer 200 with no body (Polaris returns 327KB of framework containing the word 'voice' zero times), exactly like every HIG and Material row in this file; the Carbon row is real prerendered HTML.

name: Wireframe
definition: A screen drawn as structure only: blocks where the content goes, a crossed box for an image, ruled lines for text, with no colour or type decided yet.
useWhen: settling what goes where before deciding how any of it looks

sources.title: NN/g: UX Prototypes, Low Fidelity vs. High Fidelity
NN/g: Prototypes vs Wireframes in UX Projects

notes: CATEGORY QUESTION for canonicalize, and it is the finding of the whole 'Mockup / Mock UI' wish: the three-word ladder (wireframe, mockup, prototype) is a family of REPRESENTATIONS, and none of the ten categories is about representations. They are filed in pattern together, as the least-wrong home and because round 24's lesson was to keep a family in one category rather than split it; layout was the alternative for this record alone and was refused precisely because it would have split the three. Precedent for filing a non-interface artifact: type-specimen is typography and accessibility-annotation is accessibility, both filed by material rather than by kind. ALIAS FENCE, four of them: hand-drawn-ui owns 'wireframe aesthetic' and 'lo-fi look', so the LOOK is already claimed and this record is only the artifact; skeleton-screen owns 'skeleton' and 'content placeholder'; lorem-ipsum owns 'greeking', 'dummy text' and 'placeholder text'; dot-grid-background owns 'blueprint grid', so never reach for 'blueprint'. The discrimination worth writing is against skeleton-screen: a skeleton is the wireframe the READER sees, at runtime, standing in for content on its way, while a wireframe is the one only the team sees.

name: Mockup
definition: A screen shown as it will look rather than as it will work: colour, type and real copy all settled, and nothing clickable.
useWhen: showing what a screen will look like before anything behind it exists

sources.title: NN/g: UX Prototypes, Low Fidelity vs. High Fidelity
NN/g: Prototypes vs Wireframes in UX Projects

notes: The wish's literal headword, pooled rather than substituted. Its axis against its two siblings is the one the sources agree on: wireframe and mockup differ by FIDELITY and are both static, while only a prototype is interactive, so 'static and finished' is this record's whole claim. Category question is wireframe's, shared. DEVICE MOCKUP LEFT UNCLAIMED, deliberately, and it is the more-searched sense of the bare word in stock-asset shops: a screenshot presented inside a phone or laptop bezel is a marketing artifact with different content (bezel accuracy, shadow, angle, whether the screen is real) and wants its own record, so this one must never claim 'device mockup' or 'device frame'. 'comp' alone was considered as a tail alias and dropped: the print-era word is real but a three-letter alias page is search noise, so only 'visual comp' is claimed. HONESTY NOTE for whoever authors the specimen, per SPEC 1: demonstrate a mockup of a platonic screen, never a mockup of a named product's chrome, which is the same fence bulletproof-button carries.

name: Prototype
definition: A design wired up just enough to be tried: screens linked so that a tap goes somewhere, with nothing real behind the links.
useWhen: putting a flow in someone's hands before it is built

sources.title: NN/g: UX Prototypes, Low Fidelity vs. High Fidelity
Figma Help Center: Prototyping in Figma

notes: The third of the ladder, pooled with its siblings so no one of them has to be authored against an unpooled contrast. ALIAS FENCE: never claim 'hotspot', however much every prototyping tool calls the tappable region that, because coach-mark already carries it (with 'beacon' and 'spotlight tooltip'). Category question is wireframe's, shared. FIDELITY ITSELF LEFT UNCLAIMED as the possible axis record: NN/g's article is definitional about it and it would make an excellent specimen (one screen at three fidelities), but nobody searches 'fidelity' and it would duplicate three records' content, so it is named here rather than pooled. The engineering sense of the word (a throwaway spike, or Object.prototype) is not claimed and not aliased. No design system ships a prototype, so the implementations table is honestly empty; Figma is a TOOL rather than one of the registry's five kinds, so its docs are a source and systems.json needed no new row.

name: Fake door
definition: A control that looks shipped and leads nowhere, put in the interface on purpose to count how many people want the feature behind it.
useWhen: measuring demand for a feature by shipping only its entrance

sources.title: Optimizely optimization glossary: Painted door test
Amplitude: What is fake door testing?

notes: The interface-facing half of the 'Mock UI' wish, and the one record in that wish that names something a READER can actually meet. The design content is the reveal, which is the only part of it a designer composes: the click has to land on a page that tells the truth (this does not exist yet, here is what happens next) rather than on a dead end. That is also the line it must not cross, and it is worth stating in the article rather than in a relation: a signposted fake door is an experiment, a fake door that harvests a card number for a feature that does not exist is deception, so dark-pattern is a CONTRAST and never a parent. The labor-illusion ruling of 2026-08-25 already settled the naming half of this (a 'fake-*' word is not automatically a dark-pattern sibling). Both sources are product-analytics vendor glossaries rather than design catalogs, which is where this vocabulary actually lives; neither vendor is in systems.json and neither needs to be, since these are sources and not implementations.

name: Error page
definition: The whole screen a site serves instead of the page that was asked for: what happened, in the reader's words, and the shortest way back to something that works.
useWhen: the requested page cannot be served at all, not one field failing

sources.title: NN/g: Improving the Dreaded 404 Error Message
GOV.UK Design System: Page not found pages
GOV.UK Design System: Problem with the service pages

notes: THE HONEST HOME for the 'Humorous / playful UI' wish, and it arrives with a SOURCED DISAGREEMENT that is the article rather than a footnote to it: NN/g (Nielsen, 1998) advises mitigating total failure with novelty, and the GOV.UK Design System forbids informal language on a page-not-found page outright, forbids red warning text, and forbids ever printing the number 404 at all. Both are right for their own service, and that is the only place on this site where the humour question can be settled with citations instead of taste. NAMING: 'Error page' rather than '404 page' because the slug convention spells numbers out (eight-point-grid, twelve-column-grid) and 'four-oh-four-page' is a worse URL than an alias, so the vernacular spelling is carried as the first alias and the search still lands. FENCE, a three-way one that is already half-drawn on site: error-message is the inline message under one field, error-summary is the list at the top of a form, no-results-state is a search that matched nothing INSIDE a working page, and this is the page that replaced the page. The 404-versus-5xx split is the record's own axis (you asked for something that is not here, recover by navigating, against we are broken, recover by waiting) and both GOV.UK patterns are cited for it. MAINTENANCE PAGE and COMING SOON PAGE left unclaimed as neighbouring records. govuk is in systems.json but NOT in the site schema's nine tracked SYSTEMS, so that implementation row will have to become a source when the term file is written.
